q: In landscape design, scale as a key element is best defined as what?
o: The relative size of landscape components to human scale and to other elements
The total area of the site in square meters
The drawing ratio used on the site plan
The height of the tallest tree on the site
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Scale
n: Scale here is the relative size of landscape components measured against human scale and against the other elements around them. It is a relationship, not a drawing convention or an absolute area figure.

q: Softscape elements behave over time in which of the following ways?
o: Fixed for a design life of about ten years
Dynamic — changing with the seasons, growing over time, and requiring active maintenance
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Softscape
n: Softscape elements are typically dynamic: they change with the seasons, grow over time, and require active maintenance. Being static once installed is the defining behaviour of hardscape, which is the contrast the two sections are built on.

q: Which term names the harmony or "oneness" in a design where every part feels tied together by a shared commonality?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, pp. 36–37: Design Principles — Unity (Ching, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order)
n: Unity is the sense of harmony and oneness where all parts belong together, elements being tied by a commonality of some kind. Variety is its counterweight rather than its synonym — it introduces difference to prevent monotony.

q: Decks and patios exist mainly to serve what purpose?
o: To define the property boundary and ensure privacy
To hold back soil on sloping ground
To separate garden beds from grass
To extend living spaces outdoors for dining, lounging, and social activities
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Decks and Patios
n: Decks and patios extend living spaces outdoors, making areas for dining, lounging, and social activities. Separating garden beds from grass is the work of edging and borders, a different hardscape category.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Cherry Blossom, Jacaranda, Palawan Cherry, and Fire Tree exemplify which tree category, and where are such trees typically placed?
o: Deciduous trees; on south and west facades
Evergreen trees; along boundaries as screens
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Ornamental/Flowering, Examples
n: These are the ornamental/flowering examples, often used in accent zones and giving moderate to light shading depending on foliage density. "Accent zone" is the giveaway — the tree is placed to be looked at, not to shade a facade.

q: Because proportion is fundamentally about ratios, how should it be understood?
o: The comparison of two or more dimensions
A rule of thumb for structural sizing
A perception relative to the human observer
An absolute measurement in standard units
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Proportion
n: Because proportion is inherently about ratios, it is the comparison of two or more dimensions — a relationship, not a fixed quantity. An absolute measurement is precisely what a ratio is not, which is why a proportional system can be scaled from a chair to a city block.

q: Beyond guiding circulation, what practical harm does a well-designed walkway help prevent?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Pathways and Walkways
n: A well-designed walkway connects key zones such as the house, garden, pool, or patio, subtly influences how people move through a space, and helps avoid trampling on grass or plants. Holding back soil on a slope is the job of a retaining wall instead.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Palms give high visual interest without obstructing eye-level sightlines. What benefit does this preserve?
o: Vistas, while adding a sense of scale
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Palm Trees
n: By carrying their foliage high, palms preserve vistas while still adding a sense of scale to a space. Privacy is precisely what they do not provide, since nothing is screened at eye level.

q: Proportion, subtitled "The Logic of Ratios," governs what relationship, and toward what end?
o: The perception of size against the human body; it achieves comfort
The ranking of spaces by importance; it achieves order of movement
The recurrence of elements in a pattern; it achieves visual movement
The relationship of one part to another or to the whole; it achieves Harmony
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Proportion
n: Proportion is the relationship of one part to another, or to the whole, and is used to achieve Harmony, where all parts of a building appear to belong to the same family of shapes. Perceiving size against the human body is Scale, which is the distinction most often lost between these two terms.

q: Complete the statement: the surface that mimics stone or brick at lower cost while allowing high design flexibility is ___.
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Decks and Patios, Examples
n: Stamped concrete patios imitate stone or brick at a lower cost with high design flexibility. Wooden decks are the other named surface but are valued for being warm and inviting and for elevated views, not for imitating masonry.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Pine and Spruce exemplify which tree shape, and what is that shape's best application?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The pyramidal/conical shape is triangular or cone-like, illustrated by Pine and Spruce, and gives shade at lower levels with a less broad canopy — which suits windbreaks and backdrops. Its low, dense foliage is exactly what makes it work against wind.

q: Identify the Renaissance theorists who viewed architecture as "frozen music" and applied musical-scale ratios to room dimensions.
o: Andrea Palladio and Leon Battista Alberti
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Theories of Proportion — Renaissance Musical Ratio
n: Andrea Palladio and Leon Battista Alberti held that architecture was "frozen music" and applied the consonances of the musical scale to room dimensions. Vitruvius supplied the Venustas ideal that proportion serves, but he predates the Renaissance musical ratio by some fifteen centuries.

q: Rather than merely being a "frame" for landscaping, what does the reviewer say hardscape actually defines?
o: The plant palette and its seasonal succession
The property boundary and the legal setbacks
The irrigation schedule and water demand
How a space works, how people move through it, and how comfortable and expressive it can be
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape
n: Hardscape defines how a space works, how people move through it, and how comfortable, inviting, and expressive it can be — which is why it is called essential for structure and layout, weather resistance and longevity, accessibility and functionality, and aesthetic contrast to green elements. Reducing it to a frame understates all four of those roles.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Because evergreens keep their density all year, which two functions are they best suited for?
o: Seasonal light control and passive solar heating
Producing fruit and supporting edible landscapes
Screening unsightly views and dampening "white noise" from busy roads
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Coniferous/Evergreen Trees
n: Evergreens are ideal for screening unsightly views and for dampening "white noise" from busy roads, because both jobs require the foliage to be present all year. Seasonal light control is the opposite requirement and belongs to deciduous trees.

q: A façade pairs a large plain wall with a small, intensely detailed opening, yet the composition still feels settled. Which principle explains this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Balance
n: Asymmetrical balance is the use of dissimilar elements that nonetheless carry equal visual weight, which is exactly what a large plain surface and a small intense one can do. Contrast explains why the two look different, but it is balance that explains why the composition holds.

q: Among the challenges attributed to hardscape, which one is listed?
o: It requires watering, pruning, and fertilizing
It is more expensive to install and modify
It must be replaced every season
It is vulnerable to pests and plant disease
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, pp. 61–62: Hardscape — Challenges
n: Hardscape is more expensive to install and modify, can become too dominant or sterile if not balanced with softscape, and needs proper drainage and surface planning to avoid water pooling or flooding. Watering, pruning, and pest damage are softscape problems — hardscape does not grow or get sick.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: What spacing range is recommended for large trees, based on canopy spread?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: Large trees should be spaced 15–30 feet apart depending on canopy spread. The range exists because the correct spacing follows the mature crown, not the sapling being planted.

q: Identify the architect of the Paimio Sanatorium, completed in Finland in 1933.
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Paimio Sanatorium
n: Alvar Aalto designed the Paimio Sanatorium, his breakthrough building and the origin of much of his furniture design. Eliel Saarinen is the plausible miss as the other famous Finnish architect, but he is not named in this module.

q: Which hardscape category is responsible for separating garden beds from grass and keeping edges neat?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Edging and Borders
n: Edging and borders separate different landscape zones, such as garden beds from grass, and maintain neatness. Fences and screens work at the property scale and address privacy and wind, not the boundary between a bed and a lawn.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: For a south-facing area, which tree category offers seasonal control — summer shade paired with winter sun?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Using Trees as Shade Elements — South-facing areas
n: Deciduous trees supply seasonal control on south-facing areas: shade in summer and sun in winter. An evergreen in the same spot would block the winter sun the space needs.

q: The Case Study Houses, as experimental post-war housing, were characterized by which three things?
o: Glass blocks, mechanized fittings, and mixed use
Raw concrete, monumental massing, and symmetry
Industrial materials, prefab methods, and open plans
Titanium panels, undulating walls, and digital fabrication
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Case Study Houses, Impact
n: They were experimental post-war housing using industrial materials, prefab methods, and open plans. Glass blocks and mechanized elements describe Maison de Verre, a different entry that also experimented with industrial parts but for a single wealthy client.

q: What is the stated primary purpose of a retaining wall?
o: To hold back soil, especially on sloped landscapes, and create level terraces
To carry pedestrian traffic across soft ground
To collect and store rainwater for irrigation
To define the property line and provide privacy
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Retaining Walls
n: Retaining walls hold back soil, especially on sloped landscapes, and create level terraces for planting or entertaining. Defining boundaries and providing privacy is the purpose of fences and screens.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Ornamental or flowering trees are selected mainly for what reason?
o: Their aesthetic qualities — flowers, foliage colour, bark texture, or unique canopy shapes
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Ornamental/Flowering Trees
n: Ornamental/flowering trees are chosen primarily for aesthetic qualities such as flowers, foliage colour, bark texture, or unique canopy shapes, and are used mainly for decorative value with only sometimes partial shading. Selecting one as a shade tree is a misuse of the category.

q: According to the reviewer, Villa Savoye pushed architecture toward which pair of commitments?
o: Function over form, and machine-age logic
Ornament over structure, and craft tradition
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye, Impact
n: The villa's impact is stated as a shift toward function over form and toward machine-age logic — the house understood as a rational, industrially conceived object. Regional identity and vernacular materials describe a later reaction against exactly this position.

q: What are trellises or lattices supporting climbing plants such as bougainvillea or jasmine called?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Fences and Screens, Materials
n: Living screens with hard frames are the trellises or lattices that carry climbing plants like bougainvillea or jasmine — hardscape frame, softscape surface. Wooden fences are the other timber option but are versatile styling elements rather than plant supports, and pergolas provide filtered overhead shade instead.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which two traits typically identify coniferous/evergreen trees?
o: Broad flat leaves and fleshy fruit
A single unbranched stem and a crown of fronds
Needle-like or scale-like leaves and cones
Showy flowers and a widening canopy
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Coniferous/Evergreen Trees
n: Coniferous/evergreen trees typically have needle-like or scale-like leaves and produce cones, and most retain their foliage year-round. The single unbranched stem with a crown of fronds describes palms, which are monocots rather than conifers.

q: Through masterful use of which three elements does the Salk Institute merge monumental architecture with scientific function?
o: Glass curtain walls, steel frames, and open plans
Titanium cladding, undulating form, and digital modelling
Symmetry, natural light, and raw concrete
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Salk Institute, Impact
n: Its impact is a masterful use of symmetry, natural light, and raw concrete — the last of which places it within Brutalism. The glass-and-steel combination belongs to the International Style buildings elsewhere in this list.

q: Which structural feature offers filtered shade while also serving as a vertical design anchor?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Structural and Decorative Elements, Examples
n: Pergolas and gazebos provide filtered shade and act as a vertical design anchor. Statues, columns, and planters also add vertical presence but are credited with adding elegance or cultural narrative rather than shade.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: How does a deciduous tree behave across the seasons with respect to a building, in temperate or subtropical climates?
o: Its shading is identical in every season
Sparse summer canopy admits light; dense winter canopy insulates the façade
Dense summer canopy reduces solar heat gain; bare winter branches let sunlight warm the building
Dense summer canopy reduces heat gain; dense winter canopy blocks cold winds
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous Trees
n: In summer the dense canopy shades the facade and cuts solar heat gain, and in winter the bare branches let sunlight through to warm the building — the tree does opposite jobs in opposite seasons. Blocking winter wind is the evergreen's role instead, since it needs foliage all year to work as a windbreak.

q: Where does the Centre Pompidou's "inside-out" logic reappear today, and what effect did it have on building utilities?
o: In suburban housing; it reduced their installation cost
In modern airports and tech campuses; it turned them into an aesthetic choice
In hospitals and clinics; it made them serviceable without disruption
In heritage museums and galleries; it hid them behind restored fabric
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Centre Pompidou, Modern Influence
n: The inside-out logic reappears in modern airports and tech campuses where flexibility is the highest priority, and the move turned the building's utilities into an aesthetic choice rather than something to be hidden. Its driver is flexibility, not maintenance access alone.

q: Which pathway material is noted as affordable and well-suited to rustic or informal gardens?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Pathways and Walkways, Examples
n: Gravel trails are affordable and ideal for rustic or informal gardens. Stone pavers are the near miss on informality but are described as natural and textured and popular in gardens or residential yards, and they cost considerably more to lay.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Because evergreens stay dense year-round, what is their primary use, and what winter benefit follows from it?
o: Creating windbreaks; lowering heating costs in winter
Framing vistas; improving views in winter
Producing mulch; enriching the soil in winter
Creating shade in summer; lowering cooling costs in winter
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Coniferous/Evergreen Trees
n: Their year-round density makes evergreens the primary tool for creating windbreaks, reducing wind speed significantly and so lowering heating costs in winter. A deciduous tree cannot do this because it is bare in exactly the season the wind matters most.

q: How is the ground level of Villa Savoye described relative to the rest of the house?
o: Sunken below grade as a service basement
Larger than the upper floor, forming a plinth
Relatively small and directly beneath the main living quarters
Entirely open, with no enclosed space at all
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye
n: The ground level is relatively small and sits directly beneath the main living quarters on the upper floor, which is why the house reads as a box hovering over a recessed base. It is not fully open — that describes the idea of pilotis in the abstract rather than what was actually built here.

q: What is the stated purpose of structural and decorative elements within a landscape?
o: To hold back soil and create terraces
To guide vehicles and define parking bays
To enhance style, provide support, or emphasize focal points
To separate garden beds from grass
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Structural and Decorative Elements
n: Structural and decorative elements exist to enhance style, provide support, or emphasize focal points in the landscape. Separating zones is the narrower job of edging and borders, which the module lists as its own category.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which three tree characteristics determine how effectively it blocks sunlight, reduces heat, and shapes a comfortable outdoor microclimate?
o: Species origin, soil type, and rainfall
Flower colour, bark texture, and fruit yield
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees, Their Shapes, and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
n: The shape, height, and canopy density of a tree determine its shading performance and its effect on the microclimate around it. Flower colour and bark texture matter for ornamental value, which is a separate consideration from shade.

q: The Bauhaus is credited with blending three fields while prioritizing three values. Which combination is correct?
o: Blended architecture, art, and industrial design; prioritized functionality, simplicity, and mass production
Blended history, archaeology, and restoration; prioritized authenticity, patina, and craft
Blended painting, sculpture, and theatre; prioritized expression, symbolism, and narrative
Blended engineering, agriculture, and commerce; prioritized profit, scale, and speed
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Bauhaus School, Impact
n: Its impact is stated as blending architecture, art, and industrial design while prioritizing functionality, simplicity, and mass production. The last of those three values is what separates the Bauhaus from a purely fine-art school — the object was meant to be manufactured.

q: A single sculpture, fountain, or specimen tree is positioned to draw the eye to one part of a garden. Which landscape principle is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Emphasis (Focal Point)
n: Emphasis, also called the focal point, draws attention to specific areas using distinctive features such as a sculpture, fountain, or tree. Contrast and variety may help that feature stand out, but the principle being served is emphasis.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: What two nuisances does dropped fruit create around a building?
o: It stains concrete, tiles, and parked cars, and attracts ants, flies, and rodents if unharvested
It cracks paving and lifts sidewalks
It kills the grass beneath the canopy
It clogs pool filters and blocks gutters
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Fruit-bearing Trees
n: Fruit drop stains concrete, tiles, and parked cars, and high-fructose fruit such as Mango attracts ants, flies, and rodents when it is not harvested. Clogged filters are the ornamental tree's fine leaf litter, a different complaint.

q: Which pair of architects is credited with designing the Seagram Building?
o: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building
n: Mies van der Rohe designed the Seagram Building with Philip Johnson. Piano and Rogers are the closest trap in this module because they are the other named pair, but their building is the Centre Pompidou.

q: A designer repeats the same shrub, paving colour, and path width along a garden walk. Which landscape principle is at play?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Rhythm
n: Rhythm creates movement and flow by repeating elements such as plants, colors, or paths. Unity is the close call, but unity is about a consistent theme overall, while rhythm is specifically about repetition producing movement.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Why does a deciduous tree's dry-season behaviour make it well suited to passive solar design?
o: Because it allows sunlight to pass through after shedding its leaves
Because it flowers and improves the view from inside
Because it holds moisture in its canopy and cools by evaporation
Because it deepens its roots and stabilises the soil
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: In the dry season the tree sheds its leaves and lets sunlight pass through, which is exactly the seasonal switching passive solar design depends on. In summer the same tree gives dense canopy shade, so one plant supplies both conditions without any mechanism.

q: Maison de Verre made innovative use of glass blocks, steel, and industrial detailing. What unusual mix of uses did it contain?
o: A residence combined with a medical office, using mechanized elements
A school combined with workshops, using a steel frame
A gallery combined with a library, using movable partitions
A residence combined with an artist's studio, using top lighting
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Maison de Verre, Impact
n: The building combined a residence and a medical office and used mechanized elements to make the two coexist. That mixed programme is exactly why the house is later credited with influencing mixed-use buildings.

q: Which landscape principle ensures elements are appropriately sized relative to one another and to the space as a whole?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Proportion
n: Proportion in landscape design ensures the size of elements relates appropriately both to one another and to the overall space. It is about relative sizing, whereas emphasis is about drawing attention to one area.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Mango, Guava, Avocado, and Star Apple exemplify which tree category, and what dual purpose does it serve?
o: Deciduous trees; summer shade plus winter sun
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Fruit-bearing, Examples
n: These are the fruit-bearing examples, whose dual purpose is shade plus food, and whose wide canopies suit garden areas and backyards. The dual purpose is what distinguishes the category from every other type in this list.

q: Unité d'Habitation delivered high-density housing under which concept, and what three features did it introduce?
o: The "organic city"; irregular plots, winding streets, and courtyards
The "garden city"; detached villas, hedgerows, and allotments
The "vertical city"; modular units, communal spaces, and rooftop gardens
The "linear city"; transit spines, ribbon blocks, and service roads
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Unité d'Habitation, Impact
n: The building is high-density housing conceived as a "vertical city," introducing modular units, communal spaces, and rooftop gardens — a whole town's worth of functions stacked into one slab. The garden city is the opposite proposition: low density spread horizontally.

q: Which garden, noted for native Cordillera plants and traditional huts, serves as the tropical garden example?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Tropical Gardens, Example
n: The Baguio Botanical Garden is the tropical garden example, highlighting native Cordillera plants and traditional huts. Despite its name it is classed here as tropical rather than botanical — the Singapore Botanic Gardens holds that slot.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which list correctly gives examples of deciduous trees?
o: Cherry Blossom, Jacaranda, Palawan Cherry, Fire Tree
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous Trees, Examples
n: The deciduous examples are Maple, Oak, Narra, Mahogany, and Acacia. Cherry Blossom and Jacaranda also drop their leaves, but the module lists them under ornamental/flowering trees because they are chosen for their bloom rather than their shade cycle.

q: Unité d'Habitation, built in France in 1952, is associated with which architectural movement?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Unité d'Habitation
n: The entry marks Unité d'Habitation as Brutalism, the movement its raw concrete surfaces helped launch. Postmodernism arrives two decades later as a reaction against precisely this kind of building.

q: Gardens reflect philosophies such as Zen, Renaissance, and Islamic design, and are used in healing spaces such as which two settings?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Garden — Cultural and Emotional Impact
n: Gardens evoke calmness, beauty, and reflection, and are used in healing spaces such as hospitals and temples. The pairing is deliberate — one heals the body, the other the spirit, and the garden serves both.

q: For what environmental benefit are rain gardens, green roofs, and permeable surfaces cited?
o: Managing stormwater by reducing runoff and preventing flooding
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Environmental Benefits
n: Rain gardens, green roofs, and permeable surfaces manage stormwater, reducing runoff and preventing flooding. This is the same reasoning that recommends permeable pavers for a driveway.

q: What design move allowed the Farnsworth House to maximize its usable interior space?
o: With sliding partitions that subdivide the plan at night
With an open floor plan and a single terrace overhung to one side
With a split-level section and mezzanine
With a compact core and radiating cellular rooms
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House
n: The interior maximized space through an open floor plan, with a single terrace overhung to one side. Sliding partitions would reintroduce the interior divisions the design deliberately eliminated.

q: Which world-renowned dry landscape garden, meant for contemplation, serves as the Zen garden example?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Japanese Zen Gardens, Example
n: Ryoan-ji Garden in Kyoto is the example of a Japanese Zen garden — a world-renowned dry landscape garden meant for contemplation. "Dry landscape" is the defining phrase: the garden depicts water without containing any.

q: In what way does landscaping "frame the structure"?
o: Trees are placed to obscure unattractive elevations
Hedges enclose the building on all four sides
Planting boxes are attached to the façade itself
Trees, plants, and walkways guide the eye to architectural highlights like entryways or facades
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping in Architecture — Aesthetic Enhancement
n: Framing the structure means trees, plants, and walkways guide the eye toward architectural highlights such as entryways or facades. The landscape is directing attention to the building, which is the opposite of screening it.

q: Who is the architect behind Villa Savoye?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye
n: Le Corbusier is the architect of Villa Savoye, the building in which his Five Points of Architecture are most completely realised. Mies van der Rohe is the closest confusion because he too worked in the International Style, but his residential statement in this module is the Farnsworth House.

q: Which garden is cited as the formal-garden example, expressing power and control through monumental design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Formal Gardens, Example
n: The Versailles Gardens in France are the formal garden example, displaying power and control through monumental landscape design. Monet's Garden is also French but is listed as the water garden example, built on an entirely different premise.

q: Which two elements are credited with reducing noise pollution from streets or neighbouring properties?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Functional Extension of Space
n: Plants and earth berms reduce noise pollution from streets or neighboring properties. Fences appear earlier in the module, but only reduce noise when they are themselves lined with dense vegetation or sound-absorbing panels.

q: Which software made the Guggenheim Bilbao's complex, undulating titanium forms achievable?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, pp. 35–36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
n: The undulating titanium surfaces were only buildable through advanced aerospace software, CATIA, which is why the museum marks the beginning of the digital revolution in architecture. Ordinary 2D drafting could not describe those geometries at all, let alone fabricate them.

q: Beyond geometric layouts, symmetry, axial paths, and trimmed hedges, what two further qualities are attributed to formal gardens?
o: They are high maintenance and create a sense of wildness
They are high maintenance and create a sense of order and prestige
They are low maintenance and create a sense of tranquility
They are low maintenance and create a sense of discovery
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Formal Gardens, Design Elements
n: Formal gardens are high maintenance — trimmed hedges and precise paths do not stay precise by themselves — and they create a sense of order and prestige. A sense of discovery is what the informal garden aims at instead.

q: Under psychological and emotional impact, what benefit do green spaces provide for well-being?
o: They improve sleep by lowering indoor humidity
They reduce stress, enhance mood, and support mental clarity
They shorten the perceived duration of a commute
They increase alertness by raising ambient noise
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Psychological and Emotional Impact
n: Green spaces reduce stress, enhance mood, and support mental clarity — the three effects listed under promoting well-being. These are psychological outcomes, distinct from the environmental benefits listed separately.

q: The Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, opened in Spain in 1997, was designed by whom?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
n: Frank Gehry designed the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Its titanium forms are the signature by which his work is usually identified.

q: Ride safety, fantasy architecture, and immersive storytelling are design considerations belonging to which park type?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Theme Parks
n: Theme parks function for entertainment and commercial recreation, and their design considerations are ride safety, fantasy architecture, and immersive storytelling. They are the only park type in this list whose purpose is explicitly commercial.

q: By roughly how much can good landscaping raise a property's real estate value?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Property Value and Identity
n: A well-landscaped property can boost value by up to 15–20%. The figure is worth memorising exactly, since adjacent ranges are the obvious traps in an exam item.

q: Over what span were the Case Study Houses built in the USA, and who designed the most famous of them, House #8?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, pp. 34–35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Case Study Houses
n: The programme ran from 1945 to 1966 and involved multiple architects including Charles and Ray Eames, with Case Study House #8 credited to Charles Eames. The dates matter: the whole point of the programme was that it answered the post-war moment.

q: A small-scale space carved from a single vacant lot or a small city-block corner, functioning as a micro-retreat, is which park type?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Pocket Parks
n: Pocket parks are small-scale spaces created on a single vacant lot or a small corner of a city block, functioning as micro-retreats in dense cities. The urban park is the near miss but is defined as a multifunctional green space at a far larger scale.

q: In commercial buildings or institutions, what does the surrounding landscape typically reflect?
o: The identity or values of the organization
The construction budget of the project
The seasonal climate of the region only
The zoning classification of the lot
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Property Value and Identity
n: In commercial buildings or institutions the landscape reinforces brand or character by reflecting the identity or values of the organization. The landscape is doing communicative work, much as architectural character does for the building itself.

q: In breaking from the "white box" of late modernism, what did the Centre Pompidou do with its mechanical services?
o: Buried them in a basement plant room
Distributed them within a raised access floor
Color-coded them and placed them on the exterior
Concealed them within a thickened double wall
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Centre Pompidou
n: All mechanical services — plumbing, electricity, elevators — were colour-coded and placed on the exterior, which is literally what turning architecture inside out means. Concealing them in a double wall is exactly the convention the building was rejecting.

q: In what way do parks promote social equity?
o: By reserving zones for local residents
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Park — Key Characteristics
n: Parks promote social equity by offering free public space, alongside being inclusive and community oriented, multi-zoned for activities such as sports, concerts, and walking, and often part of urban planning to give green relief in cities. Any entrance fee would undercut the equity argument entirely.

q: Through which two mechanisms do green surfaces help reduce the urban heat island effect?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Climate Control and Thermal Comfort
n: Green surfaces cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration and shade, which together reduce the urban heat island effect. Evapotranspiration is the active cooling half — water leaving the plants carries heat with it.

q: The Bauhaus building's feature list includes which range of colours?
o: Saturated primaries: red, yellow, and blue
Metallic finishes: bronze, copper, and brass
Earth tones: terracotta, ochre, and umber
Muted tones: white, gray, beige, and black
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Bauhaus School, Features
n: The features list gives muted colours — white, gray, beige, black — alongside flat roofs, smooth facades, cubic shapes, open floor plans, functional furniture, a steel frame, and glass curtain walls. Saturated primaries are associated with De Stijl and with Bauhaus painting, not with the building's own palette as described here.

q: Which set correctly lists the design considerations for pocket parks?
o: Efficient use of limited space, low-maintenance plants, and seating
Noise buffers, accessibility, seating, and water features
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Pocket Parks, Design Considerations
n: Pocket park design considerations are the efficient use of limited space, low-maintenance plants, and seating — all consequences of a very small site with no dedicated staff. Water features and noise buffers belong to the larger urban park, which has room and budget for them.

q: A building is recognisable as one designer's work because of that designer's distinctive style. Which character type describes this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Architectural Character — Personal Character
n: Personal Character is the unique style of the individual architect. It is the only one of the three that resides in the designer rather than in the building's use or in its cultural references.

q: Rough bark set against soft grass illustrates which element of landscape design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Texture
n: Texture is the surface quality of materials or plants, and rough bark against soft grass is the reviewer's own illustration. Form describes the outline of those same plants, which is the distinction being tested.

q: Which list gives softscape's living materials?
o: Stone, concrete, wood, metal, and gravel
Trees, shrubs, flowers, grass, vines, groundcovers, and mosses
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Softscape — Key Features, Living materials
n: Softscape living materials are trees, shrubs, flowers, grass, vines, groundcovers, and even mosses. Planters and benches are hardscape objects, even when plants are placed in them.

q: Historically, proportion has served as the main vehicle for achieving which Vitruvian ideal?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Proportion
n: Proportion has historically been the primary vehicle for achieving Venustas, the Vitruvian ideal of Delight — beauty rather than structural adequacy or usefulness. Its other two contributions are making the parts of a building feel like one family and letting the eye navigate the space with a sense of order.

q: Pathways and plant borders exemplify which key element of landscape design?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Line
n: Line defines edges, guides movement, and shapes the layout, with pathways and plant borders as its examples. Form is the near miss but refers to the shape of the plants and structures themselves, not to the edges they draw.

q: Which function is listed under softscape's role in the environment?
o: Resisting weather and extending the life of paving
Purifying air, absorbing water, providing shade, attracting wildlife, and cooling the environment
Providing structural support to sloped ground
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Softscape — Environmental role
n: The environmental role of softscape is to purify air, absorb water, provide shade, attract wildlife such as birds, bees, and butterflies, and help cool the environment. Structural support and circulation are hardscape functions.

q: Which term describes elements distributed equally on both sides of a central axis?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Balance
n: Symmetrical balance is the equal distribution of elements on both sides of a central axis. Asymmetrical balance also achieves equilibrium, but by using dissimilar elements of equal visual weight rather than matching ones.

q: Which landscape element sets mood, adds visual interest, and shifts with the seasons?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Colour
n: Colour sets mood and visual interest and affects how the landscape reads across the seasons. Light is a separate element in this list, concerned with highlighting features and ensuring safety.

q: Aside from plants, what other organic components does the reviewer count under softscape?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Softscape — Key Features, Organic components
n: Softscape organic components include not just the plants but also soil types, compost, and mulch. Gravel is a hardscape material even though it is loose, because it is non-living.

q: A line is divided so that the ratio of the whole to its larger part equals the ratio of the larger part to the smaller. Which proportioning system does this describe?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Theories of Proportion — Golden Section
n: That division is the definition of the Golden Section, a mathematical ratio found in nature and thought to be inherently pleasing to the human eye. The Modulor is the near miss, since Le Corbusier built it partly on the Golden Section — but the Modulor adds the human body to the arithmetic.

q: Metal cages filled with rocks, giving an industrial and rugged look, describe which retaining-wall material?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Retaining Walls, Materials
n: Gabion walls are metal cages filled with rocks and read as industrial and rugged. Concrete blocks are the other engineered option, valued instead for being modular, easy to stack, and long-lasting.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Along driveways or walkways, which tree form is recommended, and for what reason?
o: Weeping forms, for a soft ambiance
Round or spreading forms, to give the widest shade
Columnar or vase-shaped forms, to avoid blocking paths
Pyramidal forms, to act as a windbreak
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Using Trees as Shade Elements — Driveways or walkways
n: Columnar or vase-shaped trees suit driveways and walkways because their form keeps the path clear at ground level. A round spreading canopy would give more shade but would obstruct the very circulation route it lines.

q: What is the name for the point of interest a design strategy creates to make one element stand out and capture attention?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Emphasis
n: Emphasis creates a point of interest called a "focal point," which captures attention and prevents a design from appearing flat or directionless. The module is a different idea entirely — the basic unit of a proportioning system.

q: Which set of materials is used in hardscape?
o: Turf, moss, bark chips, and straw
Stone, concrete, wood, metal, bricks, tiles, and gravel
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Hardscape — Key Features, Materials
n: Hardscape materials are stone, concrete, wood, metal, bricks, tiles, and gravel. Peat, compost, and loam are soil and organic components, which the module classes under softscape.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: What kind of sun shading do evergreens provide, and for which areas are they best suited?
o: Seasonal shading; areas needing winter sun
Dappled shading; areas needing filtered light
Overhead-only shading; areas needing lateral views
Consistent sunshade throughout the year; areas needing constant shading or privacy
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Coniferous/Evergreen, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: Evergreens give consistent sunshade throughout the year, making them best for areas needing constant shading or privacy. Dappled shade is what palms produce, and seasonal shading is the deciduous property.

q: Under contrast, which term names the use of different elements to add visual interest and avoid monotony?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Contrast, Variety
n: Variety is the use of different elements to create visual interest and prevent monotony. Juxtaposition is the neighbouring term but means something narrower — the act of placing elements close together for comparison.

q: Water features balance the solidity of a landscape with which two qualities?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Water Features
n: Water features balance the landscape's solidity with movement and reflection, significantly elevating its serenity, and they enhance sensory experience while serving as a visual centerpiece. Mass and permanence describe what the rest of the hardscape already supplies.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: In what way does leaf type affect the shade a tree provides?
o: Only leaf colour, not leaf type, affects light transmission
Broad leaves give dappled light; needle-like leaves block more sunlight
Leaf type has no measurable effect on shade quality
Broad leaves block more sunlight; small or needle-like leaves give dappled or filtered light
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: How Trees Provide Effective Sun Shading — Leaf Type and Arrangement
n: Broad leaves block more sunlight, while small or needle-like leaves offer dappled or filtered light. This is the same mechanism that makes palms and fine-leaved ornamentals poor primary shade trees.

q: The Modulor reconciles the Golden Section with the human body. What measurement did Le Corbusier base it on?
o: A man with an arm raised, 2.262 meters
A man with arms outstretched, 1.829 meters
A man of average height standing, 1.750 meters
A man seated at a desk, 1.130 meters
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Theories of Proportion — The Modulor
n: Le Corbusier developed the Modulor from a man with an arm raised, 2.262 meters, producing a standardized modular system applicable to everything from a chair to a city block. It is a 20th-century attempt to reconcile the mathematics of the Golden Section with the physical realities of the body.

q: Which grouping names only built elements of hardscape?
o: Walkways, patios, retaining walls, and pergolas
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Hardscape — Key Features, Built elements
n: Built elements of hardscape include walkways, patios, retaining walls, pergolas, decks, driveways, fences, fire pits, and water features. Shrubs and groundcovers are living materials and therefore belong to softscape.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which maintenance problem is specifically attributed to certain ornamental trees?
o: Their fine, needle-like leaves clog drainage systems or pool filters
Their fallen fruit attracts ants and rodents
Their fronds become projectiles in high winds
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Ornamental/Flowering Trees
n: Some ornamentals shed fine, needle-like leaves that clog drainage systems or pool filters more easily than larger leaves do. Cracked foundations and pest-attracting fruit are the problems the module attaches to fruit-bearing trees instead.

q: Which principle is defined as how an object's perceived size relates to a standard reference, usually the human body or its surroundings?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Design Principles — Scale
n: Scale is the perception of size against a standard reference, usually the human body or the surroundings. Proportion is the constant confusion here: proportion compares parts of the design to one another, while scale compares the design to something outside it.

q: Why should a driveway's material match or complement the architecture?
o: Because vehicles damage mismatched surfaces faster
Because permeable materials only work with certain façades
Because driveway materials must legally match the building's finish
Because hardscape in the front yard often sets the tone for the entire property
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Driveways and Parking Areas
n: Driveways and parking areas are functional surfaces for vehicles that also contribute to curb appeal, and because front-yard hardscape often sets the tone for the whole property, its material should match or complement the architecture. This is a design judgment, not a code requirement.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Pine, Podocarpus, Juniper, and Mango appear as examples under which tree category?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Coniferous/Evergreen, Examples
n: The evergreen examples given are Pine, Podocarpus, Juniper, and Mango. Mango is worth noting because it appears again under fruit-bearing trees — the two categories are not mutually exclusive.

q: At Villa Savoye, what secondary job did the columns rising from the foundation and supporting the building also perform?
o: They framed the roof garden's planters
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye
n: The same columns that extended from the foundation and carried the building also separated the windows on the second floor, so the structural grid is legible in the elevation. This is one continuous system doing two jobs, not a decorative mullion added later.

q: Among edging materials, which one is described as suited to larger commercial or formal spaces?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Edging and Borders, Materials
n: Concrete curbs are functional for larger commercial or formal spaces. Metal edging is minimalist and long-lasting, while brick or stone borders are decorative and durable — each suits a different scale of project.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: A tree with a wide, symmetrical canopy — such as Narra or Acacia — casts wide, even shade over large areas. Which shape is this, and where does it work best?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The round/spreading shape has a wide symmetrical canopy — Narra and Acacia are the examples — and gives wide even shade over large areas such as yards, plazas, and parks. The oval/umbrella shape is the near miss, but it is slightly taller than wide and gives less horizontal coverage.

q: The Farnsworth House exemplifies the International Style through which two features?
o: Industrial materials such as steel and glass, and open interior spaces
Applied historical ornament and axial symmetry
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House, Impact
n: The International Style is characterised here by the use of industrial materials like steel and glass and an emphasis on open interior spaces, both of which the house states in their purest form. Exposed and colour-coded services describe High-Tech architecture at the Centre Pompidou instead.

q: Which fencing material is described as formal, secure, and commonly used in heritage designs?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Fences and Screens, Materials
n: Metal or wrought iron fences are formal and secure and are often used in heritage designs. Wooden fences are the flexible alternative — rustic, modern, or cottage-like depending on styling — but they do not carry the same formality.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Italian Cypress and palms illustrate which tree shape, and what is its main use?
o: Vase-shaped; layered plantings in small gardens
Columnar; vertical framing, borders, and lining walkways
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The columnar shape is tall and narrow, illustrated by Italian Cypress and palms, and gives limited shade — its value is vertical framing along borders and walkways. Choosing it for shade misreads what the form is for.

q: Which movement did the Centre Pompidou pioneer, and what did relocating the services to the exterior enable inside?
o: High-Tech architecture; massive flexible interior spaces
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Centre Pompidou, Impact
n: It pioneered High-Tech architecture, celebrating the "machine" of the building, and clearing the services out of the interior left massive flexible spaces that could be reconfigured for any exhibition. Brutalism is the near miss chronologically, but its interest was mass and raw concrete rather than exposed servicing.

q: How do a deck and a patio differ from one another?
o: Decks are elevated and made of wood or composite; patios are ground-level and made of stone, brick, or concrete
Decks are roofed; patios are always open to the sky
Decks are private; patios are public
Decks are ground-level and made of stone; patios are elevated and made of wood
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Decks and Patios
n: Decks are typically elevated and made of wood or composite materials, while patios are ground-level and built from stone, brick, or concrete. Both must still consider drainage, sunlight exposure, and furniture layout, so the difference is level and material, not care taken.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Under seasonal behaviour, how do deciduous and evergreen trees differ?
o: Both allow passive heating in colder months
Neither varies its shading across the year
Deciduous trees block consistently; evergreens allow passive heating in winter
Deciduous trees allow passive heating during colder months; evergreens are consistent blockers
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: How Trees Provide Effective Sun Shading — Seasonal Behavior
n: Deciduous trees allow passive heating during colder months once their leaves are gone, while evergreens remain consistent blockers year-round. Choosing between them is really a choice about whether winter sun is wanted or not.

q: Who designed the Farnsworth House?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House
n: Mies van der Rohe designed the Farnsworth House, making it his second entry in this landmark list alongside the Seagram Building. Philip Johnson is the near miss — he collaborated on the Seagram and built his own glass house, but the Farnsworth is Mies alone.

q: Which water feature is described as possibly containing aquatic plants, koi fish, or lily pads?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 63: Hardscape — Water Features, Examples
n: Ponds may include aquatic plants, koi fish, or lily pads. They are the still-water option in the list, whereas fountains and waterfalls are both defined by movement.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Unstructured, wild growth — as illustrated by Wild Guava — giving shade that varies by size and reads as uneven yet rustic, describes which tree shape?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The irregular/natural shape has unstructured or wild growth, with shade that varies by size and reads as uneven but rustic, suiting forested settings and naturalistic gardens. The unevenness is the point in an informal scheme rather than a defect.

q: To which earlier building is the Farnsworth House called the residential answer?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House
n: The reviewer calls the house the residential answer to the Barcelona Pavilion — Mies translating that pavilion's open, flowing, minimal composition into a dwelling. Villa Savoye is a different architect's residential manifesto and not the reference point named here.

q: Which pathway material is described as classic and patterned, often seen in colonial or traditional settings?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Pathways and Walkways, Examples
n: Brick walkways are classic, patterned paths often used in colonial or traditional settings. Concrete paths are the practical alternative — durable and customizable with stamping or staining — but the traditional association belongs to brick.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which of the following characterises a deciduous tree?
o: It has only one embryonic leaf in its seed
Its seasonal cycle causes it to shed all its leaves for part of the year
It produces cones instead of flowers
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous Trees
n: Deciduous trees are characterized by their seasonal cycle, shedding all their leaves for part of the year. Retaining foliage year-round is the evergreen habit, and the single embryonic leaf is what makes palms monocots.

q: Which architects designed the Centre Pompidou in Paris, completed in 1977?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Centre Pompidou
n: Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers designed the Centre Pompidou. Foster and Grimshaw are the plausible miss as the other British High-Tech architects, but the Pompidou is Piano and Rogers.

q: Beyond their practical role, retaining walls add vertical dimension and visual interest. What can they also double as?
o: Informal seating or raised garden beds
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 62: Hardscape — Retaining Walls
n: Retaining walls can double as informal seating or raised garden beds, which is why they are described as more than merely practical. The reviewer treats this as a design opportunity rather than an engineering afterthought.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which planting strategy is recommended for energy savings through seasonal light control, and what should it be paired with for layered cooling?
o: Ornamentals near windows; combined with pergolas
Evergreen trees near windows; combined with paving and gravel
Palms near windows; combined with water features
Deciduous trees near windows; combined with shrubs and groundcovers
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: Deciduous trees near windows deliver seasonal light control and therefore energy savings, and combining them with shrubs and groundcovers produces layered cooling effects. An evergreen at a window would block useful light in every season.

q: Which architects designed Maison de Verre, built in France in 1932?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Maison de Verre
n: Maison de Verre is the work of Pierre Chareau and Bernard Bijvoet. The name — "house of glass" — points to the glass-block wall that is its defining move.

q: What role do the guiding principles of landscape design generally serve?
o: Binding regulations enforced by the local government
Guidelines to create aesthetically pleasing, functional, and sustainable outdoor spaces
A planting schedule for each season of the year
A fixed sequence of construction stages
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture
n: The principles are guidelines for creating outdoor spaces that are aesthetically pleasing, functional, and sustainable — all three at once. They are design guidance, not statutory regulation, so they inform judgment rather than compel compliance.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which tree shape has a dome-like top, is slightly taller than it is wide, and offers good overhead shade but less horizontal coverage?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Tree Shapes and Their Sun Patterns
n: The oval/umbrella shape is dome-topped and slightly taller than wide, with Mango and Rain Tree as examples, and it is best for driveways and patios. Its shade falls mostly straight down, which is why horizontal coverage is limited.

q: Who is credited as the architect of the Salk Institute?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Salk Institute
n: Louis Kahn designed the Salk Institute. Alvar Aalto is the closest confusion in this list because he is the module's other architect of a scientific or medical institution — the Paimio Sanatorium.

q: In landscape balance, harmony is achieved through consistent elements and themes across the design. Which principle is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Principles in Landscape Architecture — Unity
n: Unity in landscape design is achieving harmony through consistent elements and themes across the whole landscape. Simplicity is the near miss, but it is about avoiding clutter rather than about consistency of theme.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: Which two environmental services do deciduous trees' broad leaves perform — one while growing, one after falling?
o: They fix nitrogen while growing and acidify the soil after falling
They filter particulate matter and produce oxygen while growing, and create natural mulch after falling
They absorb noise while growing and control erosion after falling
They store carbon while growing and suppress weeds after falling
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous Trees
n: Broad deciduous leaves are highly effective at filtering particulate matter and producing oxygen during the growing season, and once shed they become natural mulch that returns nutrients to the soil. The leaf-fall that seems like a nuisance is doing useful work on the ground.

q: The Farnsworth House was pared down to which three basic elements?
o: One floor, concrete shell, and clerestory strips
Three floors, steel frame, and stone cladding
One floor, steel frame, and glass curtain walls
Two floors, timber frame, and brick infill
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House
n: The house was reduced to one floor, a steel frame, and glass curtain walls — the minimum kit needed to make a shelter. Any masonry infill would defeat the transparency that is the whole argument of the building.

q: Which garden, inspired by a famous painting series and combining water with floral beauty, is the water garden example?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Gardens — Water Gardens, Example
n: Monet's Garden at Giverny is the water garden example, inspired by his Water Lilies series and blending water and floral beauty. The garden and the paintings shaped one another, which is why it is remembered as both a landscape and a subject.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: On which sides of a building should broad-leaf deciduous trees be positioned to block the strongest afternoon sun?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Types of Trees — Deciduous, Effectiveness in Sun shading
n: Broad-leaf deciduous trees belong on the South and West sides, where the most intense afternoon sun strikes. The North side receives the least direct sun and is therefore the weakest place to spend a shade tree.

q: Villa Savoye was extremely influential within which movement, and shaped what kind of later design?
o: The Brutalist movement; mass public housing
The International Modern movement; minimalist residential design
The Arts and Crafts movement; handcrafted cottage design
The Deconstructivist movement; sculptural museum design
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye, Modern Influence
n: The villa was extremely influential in the International Modern movement and went on to shape minimalist residential design. Brutalism and mass housing belong to Le Corbusier's later Unité d'Habitation, a different entry in the same list.

q: A garden uses clipped hedges (topiary) and precise paths along a clear central axis. What is it demonstrating?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Formal Gardens
n: Formal gardens are characterized by symmetry, geometric shapes, and a clear central axis, and use topiary and precise paths to demonstrate human control over nature. Mimicking the romanticized countryside is the informal garden's aim, which is the exact opposite intention.

s: Types of Trees and Effectiveness in Sun Shading
q: The Fire Tree's bright red is cited as an example of ornamentals being used for what purpose?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 65: Types of Trees — Ornamental/Flowering Trees
n: Ornamentals are used to frame vistas or signify entryways, with the Fire Tree's red as the module's own illustration, and their colour and texture contribute to the "sense of place" and to user well-being. Windbreaks call for year-round density, which is an evergreen job.

q: In which country does Villa Savoye, completed in 1931, stand?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye
n: Villa Savoye was built at Poissy in France and is dated 1931 in the reviewer's landmark list. Switzerland is the near miss for the wrong reason — it is Le Corbusier's birthplace, not the site of the villa.

q: A garden treats water as its central design and ecological feature, employing ponds, aquatic plants, koi, and reflections. Which garden type is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Gardens — Water Gardens
n: Water gardens highlight water as the central design and ecological element, using ponds, aquatic plants, fish such as koi, and reflections. The Zen garden is the deliberate contrast: it evokes water symbolically through raked sand and uses none at all.

q: Pathways, plantings, and focal points guide movement and mark entrances or destinations. Which landscaping function does this describe?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Functional Extension of Space
n: Wayfinding and circulation is the function in which pathways, plantings, and focal points guide movement and mark entrances or destinations. Outdoor rooms is the near miss but concerns defining zones, not directing movement between them.

q: Aalto wanted the sanatorium itself to contribute to the healing process. What did he like to call the building?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Paimio Sanatorium
n: Aalto liked to call the building a "medical instrument" — a device that treats, not merely a container for treatment. "A machine for living" is the near miss, but that is Le Corbusier's phrase for the house.

q: How is a garden defined within this module?
o: An intentionally cultivated area primarily focused on plants, aesthetics, and beauty
A protected tract managed for biodiversity
A large planned area of land open to the public for recreation
Any vegetated area left in its natural state
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Garden
n: A garden is an intentionally cultivated area primarily focused on plants, aesthetics, and beauty; it may be private or public, and its design often carries symbolic, cultural, or meditative meaning. A large planned area open to the public for recreation is the definition of a park, which is the contrast this section is built around.

q: To which green building certifications is landscaping said to be integral?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Integration and Sustainability in Design
n: Landscaping is integral to green building certifications such as LEED and BERDE, the latter being the Philippine rating system. PD 1096 and BP 220 are building and subdivision regulations, not green certifications.

q: Which three architects are credited with the Bauhaus School?
o: Peter Behrens, Bruno Taut, and Erich Mendelsohn
Walter Gropius, Hannes Meyer, and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe
Walter Gropius, Marcel Breuer, and Josef Albers
Le Corbusier, Hannes Meyer, and Philip Johnson
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Bauhaus School
n: The reviewer names Walter Gropius, Hannes Meyer, and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe — the school's three successive directors. Breuer and Albers were Bauhaus masters but are not the architects credited here.

q: Dense planting, a naturalistic layout, and exotic species characterise which garden type?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Tropical Gardens
n: Tropical gardens showcase lush, diverse vegetation through dense planting, a naturalistic layout, and exotic species. The naturalistic layout is what separates it from the botanical garden, which organises plants into labelled thematic zones for study.

q: Trees and pergolas cut heat gain and lower surrounding temperatures. What need does this reduce?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Climate Control and Thermal Comfort
n: By providing shade, trees and pergolas reduce heat gain and lower surrounding temperatures, minimizing the need for air conditioning. This falls under climate control and thermal comfort, the second listed effect of landscaping.

q: Who is the architect of Unité d'Habitation?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 34: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Unité d'Habitation
n: Le Corbusier designed Unité d'Habitation, which makes it his second entry in this list after Villa Savoye. Louis Kahn is the near miss because he is the module's other architect of raw concrete, at the Salk Institute.

q: Gravel, stone, minimal plants, asymmetry, and symbolism belong to which garden type's design elements?
o: Ponds, koi, aquatic plants, and reflections
Gravel, stone, minimal plants, asymmetry, and symbolism
Topiary, axial paths, and trimmed hedges
Dense planting, naturalistic layout, and exotic species
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Gardens — Japanese Zen Gardens, Design Elements
n: Zen garden design elements are gravel, stone, minimal plants, asymmetry, and symbolism. Asymmetry is the giveaway that separates it from the formal garden, whose whole logic is symmetry about an axis.

q: What reasoning does the reviewer give for landscaping enhancing curb appeal?
o: Landscaping reduces the cost of façade maintenance
Landscaped frontage is required by most zoning ordinances
Landscaped frontage lowers property tax assessments
First impressions matter, and a beautiful landscape attracts buyers, tenants, and visitors
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Property Value and Identity
n: Curb appeal rests on first impressions: a beautiful landscape attracts buyers, tenants, and visitors. It is a marketing effect on how the property is received, not a regulatory or tax matter.

q: The Case Study Houses are described as the conceptual grandfather of which movement and which approach?
o: The "Adaptive Reuse" movement and the "Kit-of-Parts" approach
The "Garden City" movement and the "Neighbourhood Unit" approach
The "Brutalist" movement and the "Vertical City" approach
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 35: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Case Study Houses, Modern Influence
n: Beyond setting the tone for mid-century modern and suburban home design, the programme is named the conceptual grandfather of the "Adaptive Reuse" movement and the "Kit-of-Parts" approach seen in modern sustainable housing and DIY modular homes. The vertical city idea is Le Corbusier's at Unité d'Habitation.

q: How does this module define a park?
o: A privately held green buffer between land uses
A large, planned area of land open to the public for recreation, rest, and social engagement
A protected wilderness closed to visitors
An intentionally cultivated area focused on plants and beauty
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Park
n: A park is a large, planned area of land, often managed by government or a private organization, open to the public for recreation, rest, and social engagement, designed for multipurpose use and integrating both natural and artificial elements. An intentionally cultivated area focused on plants and beauty is a garden — the scale and the public access are what distinguish the two.

q: Strategic planting can block harsh winds or let in winter sun. This matters especially in which design approach?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Climate Control and Thermal Comfort
n: Regulating wind and sunlight through strategic planting matters most in passive solar design, where the building relies on admitting or excluding sun without mechanical help. This is the same logic behind placing deciduous trees on the south and west.

q: What building type did the Seagram Building introduce, and in which style is it considered iconic?
o: The cast-iron loft with arched bays; Beaux-Arts
The steel-and-glass skyscraper with visible structure and a clean grid; International Style
The reinforced-concrete ziggurat with setbacks; Art Deco
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Seagram Building, Impact
n: It is the iconic International Style office tower and introduced the steel-and-glass skyscraper whose structure reads as a clean visible grid. Art Deco setbacks describe the generation of New York towers the Seagram displaced.

q: Urban parks are called the "lungs of the city." Which set lists their design considerations?
o: Minimal human interference, eco-tourism, and conservation
Noise buffers, accessibility, seating, and water features
Efficient use of limited space, low-maintenance plants, and seating
Ride safety, fantasy architecture, and immersive storytelling
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Urban Parks
n: Urban parks function as the lungs of the city and are essential for physical and mental health, with noise buffers, accessibility, seating, and water features as their design considerations. Efficient use of limited space with low-maintenance plants belongs to pocket parks, which face the same city but at a far smaller scale.

q: Which planting choice is said to support low-impact development by cutting water use and maintenance?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 67: Effects of Landscaping — Integration and Sustainability in Design
n: Native and drought-resistant plants reduce water use and maintenance, which is how landscaping supports low-impact development. Annual displays work against this, since they must be replanted and watered continually.

q: What carried the concrete slab floors of Villa Savoye?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 32: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Villa Savoye
n: Concrete slab floors resting on vertical concrete columns are what free the walls from any structural duty — the technical basis for the open plan and free façade the villa is famous for. Load-bearing masonry is precisely the system the design was rejecting.

q: An urban park functions as a multifunctional green space within a dense city. As a tool, what is it called?
o: A functional tool for public health and environmental resilience
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Urban Parks
n: The urban park is described as a functional tool for public health and environmental resilience, not merely as amenity. That framing is what justifies the space in a city where land is most expensive.

q: In which two building types does landscaping provide restorative, healing spaces?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 66: Effects of Landscaping — Psychological and Emotional Impact
n: Landscaping creates healing environments especially in hospitals and schools, where landscaped areas provide restorative spaces, and it also encourages outdoor living and increases quality of life. This echoes Paimio Sanatorium's argument that the environment itself can contribute to healing.

q: In which U.S. state is the 1951 Farnsworth House located?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 33: Significant Modern Architectural Landmarks — Farnsworth House
n: The Farnsworth House was built in Illinois in 1951. California is the tempting wrong answer because it hosts two other entries in this list — the Salk Institute and the Case Study Houses.

q: Which park, combining lakes, meadows, trails, and performance spaces within a busy city, is called a model of landscape architecture?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 68: Parks — Urban Parks, Example
n: Central Park in New York City is the urban park example, a model of landscape architecture combining lakes, meadows, trails, and performance spaces inside a dense city. Its multi-zoned programme is exactly what the definition of a park calls for.

q: Which type of architectural character comes from the cultural or historical associations a building carries?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 37: Architectural Character — Associated Character
n: Associated Character is meaning derived from cultural or historical associations — what a form has come to signify rather than what it does. Functional Character, by contrast, comes from the building's internal use.

q: Columnar trees and rounded shrubs illustrate which landscape element?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 61: Key Elements to Consider in Landscape Design — Form
n: Form is the shape of plants and structures, illustrated by columnar trees and rounded shrubs. Texture is the neighbouring element and concerns surface quality rather than overall shape.

q: A tropical planting and a Zen garden evoke different emotions and experiences. Which functional purpose of softscape does this show?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 64: Softscape — Functional Purposes
n: Mood and atmosphere is the purpose that covers how different planting styles evoke different emotions and experiences. Aesthetic beauty is the near miss but is defined as adding colour, form, texture, and fragrance, while ecological benefits covers biodiversity, stormwater, and air quality.

q: A design achieves equilibrium because its visual weight is distributed across an axis or centre point. Which principle is this?
ref: Theory of Architecture — Module 2, p. 36: Design Principles — Balance (Ching, F. D. K., 2014, Architecture: Form, Space, and Order)
